## Getting a client

### Synchronous client

```python
from payouts import PayoutsClient
from payouts.auth import Oauth2Scope
from payouts.core import ClientCredentials

client = PayoutsClient(
    oauth2=ClientCredentials[Oauth2Scope](client_id="YOUR_CLIENT_ID", client_secret="YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET"),
    environment="production",
)

# TODO: call endpoints here -- see api-reference.md

client.close()
```

Alternatively, scope it — `with PayoutsClient(...) as client:` closes the pool on exit.

### Asynchronous client

```python

from payouts import AsyncPayoutsClient
from payouts.auth import Oauth2Scope
from payouts.core import ClientCredentials


async def main() -> None:
    client = AsyncPayoutsClient(
        oauth2=ClientCredentials[Oauth2Scope](client_id="YOUR_CLIENT_ID", client_secret="YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET"),
        environment="production",
    )
    # TODO: call endpoints here, awaiting each -- see api-reference.md
    await client.aclose()


run(main())
```

Alternatively, scope it — `async with AsyncPayoutsClient(...) as client:` closes the pool on exit.

`AsyncClient` (`payouts/async_client.py`) mirrors `Client` method for method, each endpoint method a coroutine. It takes the same keywords, except that each client accepts only its own transport and — where the **Async Type** column differs — only its own flavor.

`Client` and `AsyncClient` are aliases of `PayoutsClient` and `AsyncPayoutsClient` — the names tracebacks and `repr()` show; all four import from the root.

`close()` / `aclose()` closes the transport even when you supplied one via `custom_http_client=` / `custom_async_http_client=`, and a closed client cannot be reused.

### Retries — on by default

`retry_options` left at `None` applies the default `RetryOptions` policy below, so an unconfigured client **retries**: a request whose method is in `http_methods_to_retry` is sent again when it gets a status in `status_codes_to_retry`, or no response at all, and the last outcome reaches you only once its retries are spent. A body that cannot be re-sent byte for byte — a streamed file upload — is never retried. `retry_options=0` (or `{"max_retries": 0}`) turns retrying off; a bare count sets `max_retries` and leaves every other field at its default.

`RetryOptions` fields (source: `payouts/core/retries.py`). Pass only the fields you change; each one left out takes its default:

| Field | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `max_retries` | `int` | `3` |
| `initial_delay` | `float` (seconds) | `1.0` |
| `backoff_factor` | `float` | `2.0` |
| `max_delay` | `float` (seconds) | `60.0` |
| `max_jitter` | `float` (seconds) | `0.5` |
| `status_codes_to_retry` | `frozenset[int]` | `frozenset({408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504})` |
| `http_methods_to_retry` | `frozenset[HttpMethod]` | `frozenset({"GET", "HEAD", "PUT", "OPTIONS"})` |

The wait before retry *n* is `initial_delay × backoff_factor^(n−1)` plus up to `max_jitter` of random delay, the sum capped at `max_delay`; a `Retry-After` header replaces it, trimmed to `max_delay`.

A single call overrides two of these through `request_options` (`payouts/core/request_options.py`): `max_retries` and `status_codes_to_retry`, each merged over the client's policy field by field — `request_options={"max_retries": 0}` turns retrying off for that one call and leaves every other call alone.

### Logging — off by default

Every HTTP exchange is written through the standard `logging` module under the `payouts` logger, and the SDK configures nothing itself. Set that logger's level to turn it on: INFO writes the request line and a 2xx response line, WARNING a non-2xx response line and each retry, ERROR a call that ends in an exception, and DEBUG the header dumps and the request body that the flags below turn on. Or set `PAYOUTS_LOG=info|debug` before the process starts: it sets the level, turns the three flags on for `debug`, and adds a stderr handler only where nothing listens.

`LoggingOptions` fields (source: `payouts/core/logging.py`). Pass only the fields you change; each one left out takes its default, and a name set you pass replaces its default:

| Field | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `log_request_headers` | `bool` | `False` |
| `log_response_headers` | `bool` | `False` |
| `log_request_body` | `bool` | `False` |
| `body_size_limit` | `int` (bytes) | `32768` |
| `redaction_placeholder` | `str` | `"REDACTED"` |
| `unmask_headers` | `AbstractSet[str]` | `frozenset()` |
| `mask_headers` | `AbstractSet[str]` | `frozenset()` |
| `mask_keys` | `AbstractSet[str]` | `frozenset({"sig", "signature", "access_token", "apikey", "api_key", "client_secret", "password", "refresh_token", "code", "assertion", "client_assertion"})` |

A single call is quietened through `request_options` (`payouts/core/request_options.py`): `log_level`, a `logging` level constant, is a floor below which that call's records are not written; it never turns a dump or the body on. A header value prints `REDACTED` unless its name is on the runtime's safe list, a query value unless its key is a paging name, and a form field whose key is in `mask_keys` always; a JSON body prints as sent; a response body is never logged.

## Error-handling model (read once — applies to every operation)

Every operation is reached in two response modes:

- **Parsed call.** Returns the decoded payload and raises `ApiError` on an error status, with the decoded body on `.error` and the status on `.status_code`.
- **Raw call.** Reached through `.with_raw_response`; returns `ApiResult` — `Success` or `Failure` — and never raises for an API error. Read `.payload` on a `Success` or `.error` on a `Failure`; both carry `.status_code` and `.headers`.

What `.error` holds is fixed per operation. There are two cases:

- **Case A — typed error.** The operation documents at least one error status, so `payouts/errors/` declares a union alias over the bodies those statuses map to — `RawError` is always its last arm, for any undocumented status — and `.error` is annotated with that alias. Narrow it with `isinstance`. The operation blocks name the alias and the status each arm maps from.
- **Case B — raw error.** The operation documents no error status; `.error` is `RawError` (`payouts/core/results.py`): `status_code: int` · `content: bytes` · `text(encoding="utf-8"): str` · `json(): Any`.

Core runtime types (`payouts/core/`) — public members with their **declared types**, verbatim from source:

| Type | Public members | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ApiError` — raised by every parsed call; `.error` is a Case A alias from `payouts/errors/` or `RawError` | `error: E` · `status_code: int` · `headers: Mapping[str, str]` | `payouts/core/exceptions.py` |
| `ApiResult[T, E]` — returned by every raw call; the `Success[T] \| Failure[E]` union | `payload: T` (on `Success`) · `error: E` (on `Failure`) · `status_code: int` · `headers: Mapping[str, str]` (both on either) | `payouts/core/results.py` |
| `RawError` | `status_code: int` · `content: bytes` · `text(encoding="utf-8"): str` · `json(): Any` | `payouts/core/results.py` |

Typed error bodies (the arms of a Case A alias) are ordinary models — no special handling. The operation's **Type sources** table gives the module that declares each one; read field names, declared types and JSON aliases there, as for any other model.

```python
try:
    response = client.payouts.payouts_get("some example string")
except ApiError as e:
    # Case A — typed error: e.error is PayoutsGetErrorBody
    if isinstance(e.error, Error):
        # Handle 404, 500
        print(e.error)
    if isinstance(e.error, RawError):
        # Any other error status
        print(e.status_code, e.error.text())
```

**Raw (`.with_raw_response`) variants: present on every operation** — the same call returns `ApiResult` instead of raising, with the same body on `Failure.error`. Of **4 operations**, **4 are Case A (typed)** and **0 are Case B (raw)**.

## Models — where they live, how to build them

**Shapes live only in the source.** Every module under `payouts/models/` declares one type plus its input companion, and every module under `payouts/errors/` one alias plus the mapper that builds it; no two share a name. Take a type's module from the operation's **Type sources** table. When no retrieved chunk names it, the module is the type name in snake_case under the kind's directory below (`AlternateNotificationMethod` ↔ `alternate_notification_method.py`; an error alias drops its `Body` suffix: `PayoutsItemCancelErrorBody` ↔ `payouts_item_cancel_error.py`). Never grep for a type.

| Group | Count | Directory (module = `<type_name>.py`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Models (`SdkBaseModel` pydantic classes) | 32 | `payouts/models/` |
| Enums (`Enum` over `str`) — Python member names + wire values | 27 | `payouts/models/enums/` |
| Unions (plain) — `TypeAlias` over the arms | 1 | `payouts/models/unions/` |
| Error aliases (one per Case A operation) | 4 | `payouts/errors/` |

Conventions: a model is a `SdkBaseModel` (pydantic) class; in this SDK every field's wire name is its Python name — no field carries a `Field(alias=…)`. An omittable field is annotated `Optional[T]` and defaults to `UNSET`, and one that may also be explicitly null is `OptionalNullable[T]`; both come from `core` and neither is `typing.Optional` — there is no `None` arm unless the spec declared the property nullable, so passing `None` to the first is a type error rather than a value that serializes.

Every model, enum and union also has an **input companion**, exported beside it from the same package (`AlternateNotificationMethod` ↔ `AlternateNotificationMethodDict`). Wherever a signature names the companion you may pass either the model instance or a plain dict with the same keys, whichever reads better at the call site. An enum is a real `Enum` subclass over `str`; its companion is spelled `<Name>OrStr` or `<Name>OrInt` (`BatchStatus` ↔ `BatchStatusOrStr`) and additionally accepts a wire value this SDK version does not know. A union is a `TypeAlias` over its arms.

## Servers & auth

**OAuth2 (client credentials).** Pass `oauth2` your client id and secret; tokens come from `/v1/oauth2/token` on the base URL — so `base_url="https://…"` moves token traffic too. Scopes are the `Oauth2Scope` alias.

Operation blocks name their scheme in an **Auth** bullet; an operation whose spec declares no scheme carries no such bullet.

- `AND` — every scheme listed must be configured for the call to succeed.
- `OR` — any one of the schemes listed can be used; the first one you configured is the one sent, in the order listed.

A scheme you did not configure is skipped silently rather than raising, and the request is sent anyway — so an authentication failure can mean no credential was sent rather than a bad one.

**Environments.** `environment=` selects the target environment (`payouts/server/environment.py`); this SDK's one server (`payouts/server/server_config.py`) has a base URL per environment:

| Environment | Base URL | Hosting | Override point |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `"production"` *(default)* | `https://api-m.sandbox.paypal.com` | PayPal Sandbox Environment | `base_url="https://…"` |
| `"environment2"` | `https://api-m.paypal.com` | PayPal Live Environment | `base_url="https://…"` |

Pick a row with `environment=`.
